einzeiler: How digitization and 3D printing are transforming the manufacturing industry.
kurzfassung: Digitization and additive manufacturing are fundamentally transforming the manufacturing sector by enabling real-time data usage and faster prototyping. While these technologies improve supply chain transparency and product customization, they also require significant workforce upskilling and new organizational roles. Experts from Schaeffler and Singapore University of Technology and Design discuss current applications, future potentials, and the challenges of integrating these digital tools.
stichpunkte: Schaeffler started digitalization over 20 years ago, focusing on data-driven process improvements and semi-autonomous plants.
Real-time data access improves decision-making, equipment utilization, and supply chain responsiveness.
Additive manufacturing (3D printing) accelerates product development and prototyping, mainly at the component level.
Companies face the challenge of bridging domain knowledge, requiring product designers to understand manufacturing constraints.
Singapore's Skills Future program exemplifies public-private partnerships supporting lifelong learning and professional training.
New organizational roles, such as product owners for data applications and OT security specialists, are emerging.
Future advancements in additive manufacturing at the nanoscale could enable the co-fabrication of electronics in consumer and healthcare devices.

clips.text: Access to live data enables factories to make faster choices and run machinery much more efficiently.
Although Singapore features complete additive manufacturing supply chains, everyday buyers do not notice them because applications happen mostly at the component level.

clips.hook: Predicting machine failures with big data
clips.text: Standardized global machinery combined with predictive algorithms allows companies to forecast inventory needs and coordinate directly with parts suppliers.

clips.hook: The rising vulnerability of connected supply chains
clips.text: Real-time tracking of components across international borders creates significant security risks that currently lack defined professional skill sets.

clips.hook: The resolution gap in additive manufacturing
clips.text: Traditional lithography produces electronics at sub-100 nanometer scales, whereas scalable 3D printing currently achieves resolutions measured in tens of microns.

beschreibung: This episode examines the potential, the challenges and the future of two dimensions of digital manufacturing. Firstly, the integration of digital functionality in manufacturing processes to monitor, manage and predict performance and link together participants on the value chain. And secondly, additive manufacturing or 3D printing, which is by necessity a blend of physical and digital systems. Host Pete Swabey is joined by Dr Low Hong Yee, director of the Digital Manufacturing and Design Centre at Singapore University of Technology and Design, and Klaus Mueller, chief operating officer for Asia at bearings manufacturer Schaeffler.
